headings.title: Introduction to Unit Organisation in Nursing
headings.content: Unit organisation refers to the systematic arrangement of people, resources, and workflows within a healthcare setting to achieve safe, effective, and efficient patient care. In a Nigerian hospital ward, effective organisation prevents confusion during busy shifts, reduces errors, and ensures that every member of the healthcare team understands their responsibilities. When a unit is well-organised, supplies are readily available, patient assignments match staff competency, and handover processes run smoothly. Poor organisation, conversely, leads to chaotic shifts, missed nursing care, staff burnout, and compromised patient safety. Nursing leaders must balance administrative demands with direct patient care needs to create a stable operational environment.

headings.title: Chain of Command and Organisational Structures in Healthcare
headings.content:
The chain of command defines the line of authority and accountability within a hospital. It ensures that clinical and administrative directives flow clearly from top management down to frontline staff, and that feedback travels back up safely. 

- **Chief Nursing Officer (CNO)**: Oversees nursing practice across the entire hospital institution.
- **Nursing Unit Manager / Charge Nurse**: Manages daily operations, staffing, and patient care quality on a specific ward.
- **Staff Nurses**: Deliver direct bedside care and supervise junior nursing students or assistants.
- **Auxiliary Nurses / Healthcare Assistants**: Support basic patient care activities under registered nurse supervision.

headings.title: Allocation of Nursing Resources and Personnel
headings.content: Resource allocation involves distributing available human and material assets to meet patient care demands safely. In resource-constrained settings, nurse managers must match staff skill mix to patient acuity levels. A stable ward roster considers both numbers of staff and their competencies—pairing experienced registered nurses with junior colleagues. Beyond personnel, material resource management requires routine inventory checks of essential items like IV fluids, wound dressings, and emergency drugs to prevent stockouts during critical moments.

headings.title: Workflow Design and Patient Care Delivery Systems
headings.content:
Patient care delivery systems dictate how nursing tasks are organized and assigned across a shift. Different models offer distinct advantages depending on staff strength and patient needs.

- **Functional Nursing**: Task-oriented approach where specific duties like medication administration or wound dressing are assigned to individual nurses.
- **Team Nursing**: A registered nurse leads a group of personnel in providing coordinated care to a specific group of patients.
- **Primary Nursing**: One nurse assumes 24-hour accountability for planning and directing a specific patient's care from admission to discharge.
- **Total Patient Care**: A single nurse provides all aspects of personal and clinical care for assigned patients during a shift.

headings.title: Coordination and Communication within the Nursing Unit
headings.content: Clear communication forms the backbone of a well-run nursing unit. Shift change handovers, interprofessional ward rounds, and structured documentation ensure that vital clinical information is never lost. Miscommunication can lead to medication errors, delayed interventions, and patient harm. Utilizing standardized tools like the SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) framework during phone calls or handovers helps staff transmit concise and critical patient updates effectively.

headings.title: Time Management and Priority Setting for Charge Nurses
headings.content: Charge nurses juggle clinical oversight, administrative reporting, and crisis management daily. Effective time management requires distinguishing between tasks that are urgent and those that are important. Utilizing prioritization frameworks helps ensure that unstable patients receive immediate attention while routine paperwork is scheduled for quieter periods. Delegation is another vital skill; charge nurses must assign tasks appropriately to capable subordinates while retaining overall accountability.
